did_you_know.text: Luz, the place where Jacob says El Shaddai appeared to him, was later called Bethel. The name Bethel means “House of God.”
By treating Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons, Jacob gives them a status similar to Reuben and Simeon. As a result, two later tribes are named after them.
Rachel was buried on the road to Ephrath, identified with Bethlehem, rather than in the Cave of Machpelah. Her burial place later became an important site of remembrance.
The biblical phrase “his eyes were heavy” describes eyesight weakened by age. Although Jacob could not see well, he could still welcome his grandsons by touch.

Jacob deliberately crosses his hands so that his right hand rests on the younger Ephraim. This fits a recurring pattern in Genesis, in which the younger son sometimes receives preference over the firstborn.
The blessing “May God make you like Ephraim and Manasseh” became a traditional Jewish blessing for sons. It recalls that Joseph’s two sons were counted as part of Israel’s family.

The Hebrew word shekhem can mean “shoulder” as well as “portion” or “share,” creating an interesting wordplay. It is also connected with the place-name Shechem, though the verse has been interpreted in different ways.
